## Abstract

ZZedc is an open-source Electronic Data Capture (EDC) package for R,
intended for clinical and observational research conducted by academic
groups, investigator-initiated trials, and small-to-mid pharmaceutical
sponsors. It is implemented as an R package built on Shiny and a
pluggable database layer that supports SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL,
DuckDB, and ClickHouse. This vignette is a positioning document. It
states what ZZedc is, why the architecture takes the form it does, and
which regulatory obligations are addressed by the package versus those
that remain operational responsibilities of the deploying organization.
Comprehensive technical detail and the full citation set are deferred
to the long-form whitepaper at
`docs/whitepaper/whitepaper.Rmd` and to the canonical compliance
reference at `docs/compliance/gdpr-and-cfr-part11.md`.

## The problem ZZedc addresses

Clinical data capture in small and mid-sized research programs is
served poorly by the existing toolset. Commercial EDC platforms such
as Medidata Rave or Oracle Clinical impose per-study licensing fees
and procurement timelines that are incompatible with grant-funded and
investigator-initiated work. REDCap, the dominant academic
alternative, is widely deployed but presents three constraints that
matter at the regulatory margin: its consortium license restricts
redistribution; its compliance posture is institutionally framed
rather than codified in inspectable functions; and its extension model
relies on PHP modules rather than a programming environment that
researchers already use for analysis.

ZZedc takes a different position. It is distributed under an
open-source license; its compliance claims are tied to specific
exported R functions with cited file and line locations; and its
runtime is the same R environment in which downstream statistical
work is performed, allowing the audit trail, the validation framework,
and the export pipeline to be exercised from a single language.

The design assumption is that a research group with one or two
biostatisticians and a data manager should be able to stand up a
GDPR-aware, 21 CFR Part 11-aware data capture system without engaging
a commercial vendor, while retaining the ability to read and modify
every line of the code that handles personal data. The package does
not eliminate operational obligations such as Data Processing
Agreements, signed validation reports, or breach notification
dispatch, but it provides the technical substrate against which those
obligations can be discharged.

A second design assumption shapes the package: that researchers
already write R for analysis, that they will continue to do so for the
foreseeable future, and that a data capture system written in the
same language reduces the surface area where regulated and analytical
code must be reconciled. This is a different position from the
prevailing pattern in which data capture is a vendor-managed black
box and analysis is an after-the-fact extract from that box. ZZedc
does not preclude a downstream extract; it does mean that the audit
trail, the validation rules, and the export itself are inspectable in
the language the analyst is already using.

## Architecture in one diagram and three guarantees

ZZedc is organized in five layers. The application layer is a Shiny
front-end composed of feature modules (subject management, form
rendering, query workflow, signature dialogues, privacy dashboard).
The domain layer holds the package's exported R functions, grouped by
concern: audit logging, electronic signatures, version control, the
data subject rights modules, retention, breach intake, validation, and
the rest. The persistence layer is a database adapter that translates
domain calls into backend-specific SQL. The storage layer is one of
five supported relational backends. A cross-cutting configuration and
secret-management layer governs encryption keys, study configuration,
and environment variables.

```
+----------------------------------------------------+
|  Shiny modules: forms, queries, signatures, audit  |
+----------------------------------------------------+
|  Domain functions: audit, signatures, DSAR,        |
|  erasure, retention, validation, breach intake     |
+----------------------------------------------------+
|  Database adapter: SQLite | Postgres | MySQL |     |
|                    DuckDB | ClickHouse             |
+----------------------------------------------------+
|  Configuration, key custody, environment           |
+----------------------------------------------------+
```

Three guarantees are load-bearing for the architecture and warrant
explicit naming.

The first is the hash-chained audit trail. Every audited write
through the package produces an audit row whose hash incorporates the
hash of the previous row, with a GENESIS sentinel at the head of the
chain. The function `verify_audit_integrity()` walks the chain
end-to-end and reports any break. This is the mechanism that
substantiates the 21 CFR Part 11 §11.10(e) claim of 'continuity of
record'. *Updated 2026-11-10:* until v0.8.0, this function compared
only the linkage fields (`previous_hash` against the prior row's
stored `record_hash`) and never recomputed a row's hash from its own
content, so rewriting who performed an action, which record it
touched, or when it happened went undetected while the function still
reported the chain as verified. The same fault, and the same fix
(recomputing the hash from the stored row rather than trusting
linkage alone), applied to `verify_correction_integrity()` and
`verify_version_integrity()`. All three now recompute and report
tampered rows separately from broken links. Rows written before the
fix cannot be content-verified retroactively, because the timestamp
behind their original hash was never stored; this is accurate
reporting of a real limit, not a regression.

The second is referential separation between subject identifiers and
clinical data. The schema treats subject directory tables and clinical
form tables as referentially linked but logically distinct, so that
GDPR Article 17 erasure can operate on the directory while leaving
de-identified clinical observations available for legally retained
research uses, subject to a legal-hold check.

The third is configuration-as-code. Trial configuration, validation
rules, and form metadata are stored either in versioned files or in
versioned database rows; ad-hoc administrative changes are routed
through audited workflows rather than direct database edits. This
constraint makes the audit trail a complete description of system
state changes rather than a partial one. It is also the property that
allows a deployment to be re-created from version-controlled artifacts
plus a database backup, a property that matters for both disaster
recovery and inspection-readiness.

These three guarantees are mutually reinforcing. The audit chain
records what happened; configuration-as-code ensures that the audit
chain captures all material changes rather than being bypassed by
direct edits; and referential separation gives the chain a stable
target structure on which erasure and rectification can act without
breaking record continuity.

## The five-backend database adapter

ZZedc supports five database backends through a single adapter
interface: SQLite (encrypted only with a SQLCipher-enabled RSQLite
build), DuckDB (with native file encryption), PostgreSQL,
MySQL, and ClickHouse. The motivation for supporting multiple
backends is not performance abstraction in the usual sense; it is
deployment-context match. SQLite suits single-investigator and
solo-site studies where filesystem-level backup is adequate.
PostgreSQL and MySQL suit institutional deployments that already
provide a managed relational service. DuckDB suits offline analytical
workflows where the EDC database is treated as a columnar source for
exploratory analysis. ClickHouse suits high-volume sensor or device
trials where row counts approach billions.

The adapter exposes the same domain function surface to all backends.
Schema differences (for example, autoincrement semantics, text type
limits, JSON column handling) are reconciled inside the adapter
rather than leaking into the domain layer. The trade-off is explicit:
the adapter does not expose backend-specific SQL features; deployments
that need such features must extend the adapter rather than bypass it.

A unified backend-quickstart vignette
(`backend-quickstart`) covers installation, connection pooling,
and migration steps for each of the five backends, with a
decision tree at the front and per-backend appendices.

## Audit chain and electronic signatures

The audit chain and the electronic signature mechanism together
constitute the package's posture toward 21 CFR Part 11. Both are
implemented as exported R functions with substantive tinytest
coverage.

The canonical signature path is in `R/electronic_signatures.R`.
`apply_electronic_signature()` records a signature event with
signature meaning (authorship, review, approval, responsibility),
signature statement text, signer identity, and a hash that incorporates
the signed record state. `verify_electronic_signature()` confirms a
single signature; `verify_signature_chain()` confirms a sequence of
signatures across a record's lifecycle. *Updated 2026-11-10:* before
v0.7.0, `verify_signature_chain()` had the same defect described above
for the audit trail: it checked only that each row's linkage fields
agreed with the prior row and never recomputed a signature's hash
from its content, so a signer, a signature meaning, or a signed
record's identity could be rewritten and the function would still
report the chain verified. It now recomputes each signature's hash
from the stored content and reports tampered rows separately from
broken links.

A second signature implementation exists at
`R/cfr_part11_extensions.R::create_electronic_signature` and
`verify_cfr_signature`. It is a parallel orphaned implementation
without dedicated test coverage. The canonical path governs Part 11
§11.50, §11.70, §11.100, and §11.200 claims; the orphan path will be
deprecated. This is documented openly rather than papered over.

System validation through the IQ/OQ/PQ framework
(`run_iq_tests`, `run_oq_tests`, `run_pq_tests`,
`run_validation_suite`) executes the technical portion of §11.10(a).
The organizational portion of a Part 11 validation package, which
includes a Validation Master Plan, signed validation report, and
traceability matrix to user requirements, remains an operational
deliverable produced by the deploying organization.

Record-level controls under §11.10(c) and §11.10(j) are implemented
through `R/version_control.R` (record versioning, comparison,
restoration, integrity verification, and lock or unlock) and
`R/data_correction.R` (correction request, approval, rejection,
application, override workflow, and integrity verification). Change
control under §11.10(k) is implemented through `R/change_control.R`,
covering change request, impact assessment, approval, implementation,
and verification.

## GDPR data subject rights, condensed

The data-subject-rights modules are the strongest implementation area
in the package. Each right is served by a dedicated R module with a
substantive function surface and tinytest coverage.

The right of access (Article 15) is served by `R/dsar.R`, which
covers request intake, identity verification, response generation,
and deadline tracking. Rectification (Article 16) is served by
`R/rectification.R`. Erasure (Article 17) is served by `R/erasure.R`,
including a legal-hold mechanism that reconciles the GDPR erasure
obligation with 21 CFR Part 11 §11.10(c) record-retention obligations
when both apply to the same subject. *Updated 2026-11-10:* before
v0.7.0, the hold was consulted only when an erasure item was created;
`execute_erasure_item()` checked only that the item's status was
`APPROVED`, so a hold placed after approval but before execution did
not block deletion. The hold is now re-checked immediately before
execution, not only at intake. Restriction (Article 18) is
served by `R/restriction.R`, which implements both restriction-state
storage and a processing-attempt log so that subsequent processing
can be blocked with a record. Portability (Article 20) is served by
`R/portability.R`, which generates the machine-readable export
required by Article 20(1) and supports controller-to-controller
transfer where technically feasible per Article 20(2). Objection
(Article 21) is served by `R/objection.R`.

Consent (Articles 6, 7, 9) is served by `R/consent.R`. Granular
purposes are recorded; consent withdrawal under Article 7(3) is
distinct from erasure and produces its own audit trail.

Retention (Article 5(1)(e)) is served by `R/retention.R`, with policy
definition, registration of records under policy, expiry detection,
hold and extension workflows, and either deletion or anonymisation at
expiry.

Privacy impact assessment (Article 35) is served by
`R/privacy_impact.R`, supporting risk assessment, overall risk
calculation, submission for review, and approval.

Breach intake under Articles 33 and 34 is served by
`R/breach_notification.R`. Incident reporting, status updates, risk
assessment, the 72-hour deadline check, and the timeline log are all
implemented. The functions that name themselves as notifications
(`notify_dpo`, `notify_supervisory_authority`, `notify_data_subjects`)
persist notification intent rather than transmitting it; the
operational obligation to actually communicate with the DPO,
supervisory authority, and affected subjects is described in the
'Where the package boundary ends' section below.

## Validation framework and CRF best practices

The package ships an IQ/OQ/PQ validation framework that runs as R
code (`run_iq_tests` for installation qualification, `run_oq_tests`
for operational qualification, `run_pq_tests` for performance
qualification, `run_validation_suite` for the bundled run). These
functions exercise the package's compliance-relevant code paths and
produce a structured validation result that can be archived as a
deployment artifact.

Case Report Form authoring is supported through a Google Sheets
workbook ingestion pipeline and a CSV authoring path. Validation rules
are expressed in a constrained domain-specific language that compiles
to R, with a permission and approval workflow for rule changes and
versioned history of every rule modification. Form definitions are
versioned as records, so a CRF revision creates a new version rather
than mutating the prior version.

The `content-author-guide` vignette is the working reference for
content authors; this overview omits the syntax of the validation DSL
and the authoring workbook structure.

## Deployment patterns: solo, multi-site, AWS

ZZedc supports three deployment patterns. The solo deployment is a
local installation against an SQLite backend, intended for
single-investigator studies or for development. The multi-site
deployment is a Docker image running against PostgreSQL or MySQL,
deployed to an institutional virtual machine with site-based access
control configured at the application layer. The AWS deployment runs
the same Docker image on an EC2 host with the database on RDS,
encryption keys managed by AWS KMS, and TLS terminated at an
application load balancer.

Operational details for each pattern are in the
`technical-lead-guide` vignette: AWS / Docker deployment in
Chapter 8, encryption mechanics in Chapter 5, and disaster
recovery (backup verification and audit-integrity check on
restore) in Chapter 9.

A few cross-cutting operational concerns are worth naming. Encryption
key custody is bound to the deployment pattern: solo deployments
typically use environment-variable key storage with filesystem
permissions on the key file; institutional deployments typically use
the operating system's secret store; AWS deployments use KMS. The
package's encryption utilities accept any of these key sources but do
not impose one. TLS termination is the responsibility of the
deployment's reverse proxy or load balancer; the Shiny application is
not expected to terminate TLS itself. Backups are the responsibility
of the database operator; the package provides verification helpers
that confirm audit-chain integrity on a restored copy, but does not
perform the backup itself.

## Where the package boundary ends

A regulatory-compliance package is judged in part by the honesty of
its scope statement. ZZedc does not, on its own, satisfy the
following obligations. They are listed here so that prospective
adopters can estimate the operational work required around the
package.

Encryption at rest on SQLite requires a SQLCipher-enabled build of
RSQLite. The default RSQLite distribution from CRAN does not include
SQLCipher; on it, the key is accepted and ignored, and the file is
written in plaintext. Before 2026-11-10 that happened silently (see
the encryption remediation section below); it is now detected, and
the `regulated` security profile refuses such a database. DuckDB
encrypts its files natively with `ENCRYPTION_KEY`, using only CRAN
software, and is the recommended route when encryption at rest is
required. Server backends depend on server-side encryption: zzedc
verifies it on MySQL/MariaDB by asking InnoDB whether the study's
tables are encrypted, accepts a recorded deployer attestation on
PostgreSQL (labeled as attested, not verified), and does not check
ClickHouse. Encryption support is therefore best described as
'available and verifiable on DuckDB; deployment-conditional on SQLite;
provided by the server operator and checked or attested on server
backends', not 'bundled'. AWS KMS
integration is callable when AWS credentials are configured, but no
integration test runs against a live KMS endpoint.

Outbound notification transport is out of scope. GDPR Articles 33,
34, and 19 each require an outbound communication: to the
supervisory authority within 72 hours of a personal-data breach, to
data subjects when a breach is high-risk, and to recipients to whom
personal data has been disclosed when erasure or rectification has
occurred. The package implements intake, classification, timeline
tracking, and persistence of notification intent for all three. It
does not send email, post to an HTTP endpoint, or interface with any
postal service. The functions `notify_dpo()`,
`notify_supervisory_authority()`, `notify_data_subjects()`, and
`notify_erasure_third_party()` insert rows; the controller must
satisfy the transport requirement by other means and record the
dispatch back into the system, after which timeliness can be verified
via `check_72_hour_deadline()`. This is a deliberate scope decision:
the package does not own the messaging stack.

The Article 30 register and the data minimization log have schema
present but no exported functions to write to or query them. The
international-transfer mechanisms required by Chapter V (transfer
impact assessment, Standard Contractual Clauses tracking, adequacy
lookup) are not implemented; a boolean flag and a UI label are
present but do not constitute a transfer-governance mechanism.

*Updated 2026-11-10: the paragraph below described a schema-only gap
that has since been closed; see the gap-analysis addendum's §11.10(i)
row.* User training records under §11.10(i) previously had a
schema-only presence, with no exported function to record training
events or block sign-off based on training status.
`ensure_user_training_table()`/`db_insert_training_record()` and a
real `observeEvent()` handler in the Compliance tab now record
training events from the live application; whether training status
blocks sign-off anywhere in the workflow was not re-checked for this
revision.

Multi-factor authentication is documented in `R/auth_module.R`; this
module was outside the scope of the most recent compliance audit and
its claims are unverified at the present revision.

Electronic-signature passwords are hashed with unsalted SHA-256 in
`verify_password_for_signature()`, while the application's own login
path (`inst/app/auth.R`) salts credentials via the `ZZEDC_SALT`
environment variable. The two schemes are inconsistent, and an
unsalted, single-round hash is a weak construction for a credential
that gates a 21 CFR Part 11 electronic signature. This has been
identified but deliberately not changed, because correcting it
requires a migration (existing stored signature-password hashes would
have to be rehashed under the new scheme), not a code edit; it is
recorded here as an open item rather than fixed blind.

**Audit trail gap, found and fixed 2026-11-08.** Two independent
defects had left §11.10(e) ("secure, computer-generated, time-stamped
audit trails") substantially broken, both now corrected and covered
by permanent regression tests:

1. The CRF Designer module (`R/crf_designer.R`) never called
   `log_audit_event()` at all -- confirmed by grep across the
   source. Adding, moving, or deleting a form field through
   `create_designer_form()`, `add_form_field()`,
   `add_form_field_by_code()`, `update_field_position()`,
   `delete_form_field()`, and the module's other mutators left no
   audit row. Each now logs its own `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE` event
   through a new local helper, `audit_cd_event()`.
2. Independently, and more severely: ten existing
   `log_audit_event()` call sites across `R/adverse_events.R`,
   `R/electronic_signatures.R` (two sites), `R/data_correction.R`
   (six sites), and `R/protocol_compliance.R` had been silently
   writing nothing for an unknown period before this fix.
   `log_audit_event()`'s `operation` argument has no default and is
   evaluated before that function's own `tryCatch` begins; every one
   of those ten calls omitted it, so the resulting error was thrown
   before `log_audit_event()` could catch it, and was instead
   swallowed by the *caller's* `tryCatch(..., error = function(e)
   NULL)`. The outer operation (recording an adverse event, applying
   or revoking a signature, requesting, approving, rejecting, or
   applying a correction, reporting a protocol deviation) always
   reported success; the audit row never existed. A second,
   compounding defect at the same ten sites meant that even once
   `operation` is supplied, the write would still target the wrong
   database whenever the caller passed an explicit `db_path` (as
   every test harness, and potentially a multi-study deployment,
   does) -- `db_path` was never forwarded to the nested
   `log_audit_event()` call. Both omissions are now fixed at every
   site, and `run_oq_tests()`'s OQ-003 audit-logging check
   (§11.10(a)) is noted as an incomplete safeguard against this
   specific failure mode: it calls `log_audit_event()` directly with
   `operation` supplied, so it always passed throughout, and would
   not have caught this defect at any of the ten real call sites.

A form-definition change is still recoverable only from the Google
Sheet's own edit history if the audit row is somehow lost, as
described in `vignette('promotion-tracker-add-field-walkthrough')`,
Section 2 -- but as of this fix, the normal path through
`add_form_field_by_code()` does write that audit row.

Across 50 audited features mapped to GDPR articles or 21 CFR Part 11
sections, the canonical compliance reference classifies 35 as
implemented, 8 as partial (most often because of an absent transport
layer or a deployment-conditional prerequisite), 6 as documented only
(schema present without code), and 1 as not implemented. *Note
(2026-11-10): this 35/8/6/1 split predates the remediation documented
in the gap-analysis addendum and the encryption-remediation sections
below, several of which moved an individual feature from a worse
category to a better one (for example, training records moved from
documented-only to implemented). The canonical compliance reference
has not yet been regenerated to reflect this, so the split above
should be treated as stale pending that reconciliation, not as a
current count.* We do not report a single 'compliance percentage';
the per-feature table in the canonical reference is the authoritative
substitute. Earlier internal
summary documents quoted figures of 35%, 65%, 75%, and 90% with no
shared denominator; those figures are superseded.

The dual-compliance interaction between regulatory hold and legal
hold is also worth flagging. The Shiny privacy module checks a
configuration flag and halts erasure as a 'regulatory hold'; the
legal-hold mechanism in `R/erasure.R` operates on a separate table.
There are therefore two answers to 'is this record on a regulatory
hold?' and they are not unit-tested together. A future revision will
unify them.

## Addendum: 21 CFR Part 11 Gap Analysis (2026-11-08)

Following the audit-trail defects documented above, a section-by-
section review of 21 CFR Part 11 Subpart B (§11.10(a)-(k), §11.30,
§11.50, §11.70, §11.100, §11.200, §11.300) was run against this
package's actual source, not against this document's own prior
claims or docstrings. The method was to read the function(s) that
subpart B's claimed to be covered by, exercise them where feasible,
and classify each requirement as VERIFIED IMPLEMENTED, PARTIALLY
IMPLEMENTED, DOCUMENTED-ONLY (schema or UI present, no working code
behind it), or MISSING. A recurring pattern emerged: this document
has consistently identified *that* a gap exists in the right place,
but has underestimated *how broken* the surrounding mechanism
actually is -- the same pattern already visible in the audit-trail
finding above (not merely absent in one module, but silently broken
in ten others).

| Section | Requirement | Verdict | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| §11.300(b)/(d) | Password controls (lockout, periodic revision) | **FIXED (2026-11-10)** | `authenticate_user()` (`inst/app/auth.R` -- the live login path; `R/auth_module.R`'s copy of the same function is dead code for the shipped app, never called) now counts failed attempts, locks the account after `max_failed_attempts`, and auto-unlocks after `lockout_duration_minutes`; `unlock_user_account()` adds the manual admin path (both 2026-11-09). Periodic revision closed 2026-11-10: a new `password_changed_date` column (migrated by `ensure_edc_users_table()`, backfilled from `created_date` for existing rows rather than left `NULL`) is set by every write site that changes a password (`db_insert_user()`, the self-service change-password flow, both admin reset/edit paths). `authenticate_user()` compares its age against `cfg$auth$password_expiry_days` (default 90) and reuses the existing `must_change_password` gate to force a change -- no new UI, since that gate (`change_password_module.R`) already existed for the "password someone else chose" case. |
| §11.10(i) | Training records | **FIXED (2026-11-09)** | `ensure_user_training_table()`/`db_insert_training_record()` (`R/db_users.R`) and a real `observeEvent(input$record_training, ...)` handler (`R/cfr_compliance_module.R`) replace the previously-dead button. |
| §11.10(e) | Audit trail validation coverage | **FIXED (2026-11-09)** | OQ-003 now re-queries `audit_log` for the row it claims to have written instead of trusting `log_audit_event()`'s boolean return -- the exact gap that let it pass throughout the ten-site outage. Fixing it surfaced two further bugs in the same validation functions (below). |
| §11.10(a) | IQ/OQ/PQ validation suite | **FIXED (2026-11-09); previously non-functional, not merely caveated** | IQ-005/IQ-006 and the whole of `run_oq_tests()`/`run_pq_tests()` generated an encryption key via `initialize_encrypted_database()` but never persisted it, so every one of them failed with "Database encryption key not found" in any session without a key already set from elsewhere -- the ordinary case for a deployer running the suite right after install. Separately, `get_db_adapter()` threw (and never cached a fallback) whenever `./config.yml` existed but predated the multi-backend `db_backend` schema, which is this package's own repo-root `config.yml`. Both fixed; the suite now passes end to end with no key pre-set, run from the package's own directory. *Update 2026-11-10:* IQ-003 claimed "Encryption working" while checking only key format; it is renamed and reworded. A new IQ-008 checks the deployment's storage encryption against the security profile, and under `regulated` it fails a stock-RSQLite SQLite deployment, as it should; the bundled `config.yml` now sets `regulated`, so running the suite against this repository's own demonstration database reports that failure (see "Encryption remediation, Phase 0" below). |
| §11.10(k) | Change control | VERIFIED IMPLEMENTED | `R/change_control.R` has a real create, submit, impact-assessment, approval, implementation, verification pipeline, not a stub. |
| §11.10(f) | Operational/sequencing checks | PARTIALLY IMPLEMENTED | `data_correction.R` enforces `status == "PENDING"` before approve/reject -- real sequencing, spot-checked only; not verified across every module's state machine. |
| §11.50/§11.70 | Signature manifestation and record linkage | **FIXED (2026-11-09); the function was always correct, the live app was not** | `apply_electronic_signature()`/`verify_electronic_signature()` themselves were already correct (signer name, timestamp, meaning; password re-verification at signing; SHA-256 hash chain linking the signature to the record). The gap was that `R/cfr_compliance_module.R`'s UI -- the only way to apply or verify a signature in the shipped app -- never called either one: `apply_signature`'s handler fabricated a signature id with no password check, and `verify_signature`'s handler reported "verified successfully" for any non-empty id, real or not. Both now delegate to the real functions. |
| §11.10(g) | Authority checks | **PARTIALLY FIXED (2026-11-09); previously MISSING entirely** | `require_role()` (`R/authorization.R`) is now wired into `approve_correction()`/`reject_correction()`, `invalidate_signature()`, `lock_form_design()`, and `save_user_to_db()` -- none had any server-side role check before (only incidental guards or client-side dropdown filtering a direct call bypassed entirely). A related bug found while reusing the existing `.ROLE_TIER` model: `"Data Manager"` never matched its own tier (space vs. underscore in the lookup key), silently falling back to the `Coordinator` tier -- fixed. Not yet covered: most other sensitive operations across the package were not audited for the same gap; this pass covered the four call sites the original research identified, not an exhaustive sweep. |
| §11.10(c) | Record retention | VERIFIED IMPLEMENTED at reasonable depth | `R/retention.R` has policy creation, record registration, expiry detection, legal hold, extension, and anonymize/delete-at-expiry; not independently verified end to end. |
| §11.10(d) | Access limitation | PARTIALLY IMPLEMENTED, better than this document previously hedged | `authenticate_user()` does check `active = 1` and hash-compare the password -- a real gate exists. The lockout/expiry layer is now covered by the §11.300 fix above. |
| §11.10(b) | Record-copy completeness | **PARTIALLY FIXED (2026-11-09)** | The signature and correction text reports (`generate_signature_report()`, `generate_correction_report()`) silently capped at the first 50 rows in their human-readable form, noting "... and N more" rather than reproducing them -- the json form already had everything; the txt form now does too. No single function yet assembles a complete case record (CRF data + audit trail + signatures for one subject); that remains a real feature addition, sized similarly to the UI-mounting work below, not attempted in this pass. |
| §11.100 | Signature uniqueness, non-reassignment, pre-signature identity verification | **Scoped down, not fully fixed (2026-11-09)** | Username/`user_id` uniqueness is enforced by the schema's `UNIQUE`/`PRIMARY KEY` columns plus the absence of any `DELETE` path for `edc_users`; `db_insert_user()`'s UNIQUE-constraint error now names the real cause ("already in use, possibly by a deactivated account") instead of a generic "Database error". "Verify identity before granting signing authority" as a step distinct from ordinary login is not implemented and is treated here as a deployer-operational control (an SOP, not in-app code) outside the package's boundary. (The encryption-no-op finding, previously grouped with this one as a deployer concern, was fixed in code on 2026-11-10; see "Encryption remediation, Phase 0".) |
| §11.200(a) | Two distinct identification components at signing | **FIXED as a side effect of the §11.50/§11.70 fix above; a related credential-strength weakness remains open** | Login already used two components (username + password). The missing piece was that the live signing UI never checked the second component at all, since it never called `apply_electronic_signature()`; now that it does, `verify_password_for_signature()` runs on every signature. `verify_password_for_signature()` itself hashes with unsalted, single-round SHA-256, inconsistent with the salted scheme `inst/app/auth.R` uses for login; this is a known, deliberately unfixed weakness (see 'Where the package boundary ends' below), not addressed by this fix. |

**A new finding surfaced only by actually running the live app for this remediation**, not by reading source: `inst/app/gsheets_ui_integration.R`'s `create_enhanced_ui()` -- the UI path actually used whenever no Google Sheets integration is configured, i.e. the common case -- fails on every single request with "object 'output' not found", a pre-existing, unrelated bug in `home.R`'s top-level `output$hometab <- renderUI(...)` assignment (that object does not exist at UI-generation time; `ui.R` is sourced once per app, not per session). `ui.R` catches the error and falls back to its own traditional `nav_panel` block, which is why the app has still been usable in practice -- but the "enhanced" path has likely never worked, in any deployment, for as long as `home.R` has had that line. Not fixed here (unrelated to Part 11); flagged because mounting the Compliance/Admin tabs (below) required adding them to both UI paths to be reachable at all.

Mounting `admin_dashboard_ui()` into the live app for the first time ever (confirmed by a repo-wide grep: nothing in `inst/app/` had ever called `admin_dashboard_server()`/`cfr_compliance_server()` before this remediation) surfaced a second, unrelated, previously-undiscovered defect: `backup_restore_module.R`, `audit_log_viewer_module.R`, and `admin_dashboard_module.R` itself all called bare `label(...)`/`input(...)`, which is not a function anywhere in base R, shiny, or htmltools -- every one of these UI functions had always thrown `could not find function "label"` the instant anything actually rendered them. Fixed to `tags$label()`/`tags$input()`. No test had ever called any of these UI functions before, which is exactly how this went unnoticed through every prior change to these files.

A repo-wide sweep for the same pattern (2026-11-10) found four more instances, all previously masked the same way (zero test coverage of the actual rendering code path) or hidden behind `globalVariables()` declarations that suppressed the `R CMD check` NOTE without making the calls actually work: `setup_wizard_module.R` (6 `label()`, 1 `input()`, in the never-mounted setup wizard UI); `cfr_compliance_module.R`'s `signature_verification_result` `renderUI` (2 bare `small()` calls, on both the success and failure branch -- this one is reachable from the live, mounted Compliance tab, since verifying any signature would have crashed the result display); and `instrument_import_module.R` (1 bare `small()`, in a never-mounted module). All fixed to `tags$small()`/`tags$label()`/`tags$input()`, with `small`/`label` removed from `zzedc-package.R`'s `globalVariables()` declaration now that their real cause is confirmed rather than guessed at. New regression tests exercise the actual rendering path (via `shiny::testServer()` plus `session$flushReact()` and an explicit `output$...` access, not just a direct call to the underlying data function) for each, verified to fail against the pre-fix code and pass after.

**A third finding, surfaced while diagnosing an unrelated CI failure (2026-11-10), not by reading source or running the app**: `CURRENT_DATE` is used in `R/dsar.R` (data-subject-access-request deadline comparisons) and `R/adverse_events.R` (expedited adverse-event reporting deadlines). On the DuckDB backend, `CURRENT_DATE` can require DuckDB's bundled `icu` extension, which DuckDB fetches over the network the first time it is needed and does not bundle by default. A CI runner with no route to DuckDB's extension server failed these exact queries with an "Extension Autoloading Error" rather than falling back or erroring at connection time -- the failure surfaces only when a deadline comparison first runs, not at startup. The CI instance of this was fixed by warming the extension cache once before the test suite runs (`.github/workflows/r-package.yml`), which is a CI-only fix with no effect on package behavior. The underlying risk is real for a *deployed* DuckDB backend, not just CI: if a production DuckDB instance also has no network route to DuckDB's extension server (an air-gapped or egress-restricted environment, which is plausible for a clinical-trial deployment), DSAR and adverse-event deadline queries would fail at runtime the same way. Not fixed in package code here -- it needs a deliberate choice between bundling/pre-installing the `icu` extension in the deployment image, or avoiding extension-gated date functions on the DuckDB backend entirely -- the same category of decision as the encryption-no-op and identity-verification findings above: flagged for the deploying team, not fixed blind.

**A fourth finding, more severe, surfaced immediately after the third while the CI test suite progressed further than it ever had before (2026-11-10) -- FIXED**: encrypted DuckDB database creation never actually worked on at least one DuckDB build (1.5.4.1, the version this package's CI pins). `R/db_adapter_duckdb.R`'s `connect()` and `pool()` both open an encrypted database via `ATTACH '<path>' AS zzedc (ENCRYPTION_KEY '<key>')`, which requires DuckDB's full (writable) mbedtls crypto module; that build loads only a read-only crypto module by default, so every such `ATTACH` failed outright with "DuckDB currently has a read-only crypto module loaded... ensure httpfs is loaded using `LOAD httpfs`". This is the same category of defect as the portfolio-wide "encryption silent no-op" finding (05-zzedc's own prior review flagged it as the most severe issue in the portfolio): a DuckDB deployment configured for at-rest encryption would never actually get it, on an affected build, with no caller-visible signal beyond a connection error on first use -- not a silent no-op this time, but still undiscovered until this session because no test or deployment had exercised DuckDB's encrypted path to completion before. Fixed by loading `httpfs` before the `ATTACH` call in both call sites; verified harmless on a newer DuckDB build (2.0.0) where it was not otherwise required, and verified to fix the actual failure end to end (encrypted file created, re-opened, and queried successfully).

## Encryption remediation, Phase 0 (2026-11-10)

The plan in `docs/encryption-compliance-plan-2026-11-10.md` sets
out the work needed before zzedc can claim to support deployments
subject to 21 CFR Part 11, the HIPAA Security Rule, GDPR Article 32,
and institutional encryption policies. Its premise is that a package
cannot itself satisfy those regimes, which bind the operating
organization; it can provide validated technical controls and state
which controls remain the deployer's. Part 11 does not require
encryption at rest for closed systems, but §11.10(a) validation
requires a system to do what it claims, and the package claimed
encryption it did not provide. Phase 0 removes those false claims.

**Defects confirmed by execution before the fix.** On stock CRAN
RSQLite, `initialize_encrypted_database()` returned the message
"Database created and encrypted" for a file whose header read
`SQLite format 3` and which a keyless connection could read in full.
`verify_database_encryption()` judged encryption by requiring more
than 80 percent of the first kilobyte's bytes to exceed 127; random
bytes, which ciphertext resembles, scored 0.476, so a correctly
encrypted file would have failed the check, and the check could not
distinguish encrypted from plaintext files. `set_encryption_for_existing_db()`
generated a key and a backup but never rewrote the file.
`export_encrypted_data(password = ...)` ignored the password and wrote
a plaintext CSV.

**Defects found by reading source and fixed.** The adapters'
`supports_encryption()` returned `TRUE` for PostgreSQL, MySQL, and
ClickHouse on the strength of TLS, which is not encryption at rest,
and the SQLite adapter tested for a package name (`RSQLCipher`)
rather than for a working cipher. `selective_field_export()` called
`sha256(value || key)` under the database key "field-level
encryption"; it is a non-standard, irreversible hash. An AWS KMS
failure fell back to an environment-variable key with only an
informational message. `test_encryption()` warned rather than failed
on a plaintext file. The SQLite adapter applied `PRAGMA key` after
other statements, which a cipher build rejects, and its connection
pool applied no key at all.

**A finding surfaced only during implementation.** The shipped Shiny
application never used the encryption code. `inst/app/global.R`
opens its SQLite connection pool directly with `RSQLite`, with no key
and no check, so no configuration setting could have made the
running application encrypt or refuse anything. A startup check,
`check_storage_encryption()`, now runs before the pool is opened.

**A finding about a dependency.** `openssl::aes_gcm_encrypt()` in
openssl 2.4.2 returns no authentication tag (11 bytes of output for
11 bytes of input), and a ciphertext with one bit flipped decrypted
without error. The export encryption therefore uses AES-256-CTR with
an HMAC-SHA256 tag over the whole file (encrypt-then-MAC) rather than
GCM.

**What changed.** A single setting, `security.profile`
(`R/security_profile.R`), now governs every encryption-related
decision: `development` allows unencrypted storage silently,
`standard` (the built-in default, chosen so existing deployments keep
running) allows it with a warning, and `regulated` refuses it,
including at application startup, and refuses a KMS fallback. New
configuration templates, the setup wizard, and the bundled
`config.yml` write `regulated`. Result fields report the true state
under every profile. Verification now tests the property encryption
exists to provide (unreadable without the key, readable with it) for
both SQLite and DuckDB files. `set_encryption_for_existing_db()`
encrypts DuckDB files in place, with verification before the swap,
and refuses rather than pretends on stock RSQLite. Exports are
encrypted when a password of at least 12 characters is supplied
(bcrypt-pbkdf key derivation, 64 rounds), and no plaintext copy is
left in the export directory. Identifier pseudonymization uses
HMAC-SHA256 under a key derived separately from the database key,
and is documented as pseudonymization in the GDPR Article 4(5) sense,
not encryption; its output values differ from those of earlier
versions. The validation suite gained IQ-008, which judges the
deployment's own storage under the active profile, while the
functional IQ/OQ/PQ checks run their throwaway databases under a
scoped `development` profile. Running the suite also no longer
leaves the cached database adapter pointing at a deleted temporary
file.

**Evidence.** 89 new assertions in
`inst/tinytest/test_security_profile.R` pass, including end-to-end
DuckDB encryption, in-place conversion, and tamper detection on
encrypted exports. A per-file run of the whole suite before and after
the change showed no new failures beyond one (an IQ-008 abort caused
by an empty `ZZEDC_DB_PATH` left by another test file), which was
fixed and re-verified. Five assertion failures, in
`test_change-password-module.R` and `test_home-module.R`, and one
aborting file, `test_quality-dashboard.R`, fail identically on the
unchanged code and are unrelated. `R CMD check --as-cran --no-manual`
on the changed package: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 1 note (new submission,
and one redirected URL in the content-author guide).

**What Phase 0 does not do.** The SQLite path with a cipher-enabled
RSQLite build was not executed, because no such build was available;
only its refusal path on stock RSQLite is tested. Server-backend
encryption at rest is still not verifiable; under `regulated`, IQ-008
fails such deployments until an attestation mechanism exists (plan
Phases 1.3 and 1.4). Backups are not yet encrypted by zzedc (Phase
2.1). HTTPS settings in `config.yml` remain unenforced and are now
labeled as such (Phase 3.1). DuckDB's `httpfs` extension, needed for
encrypted files, is downloaded on first use and will fail on hosts
without internet access unless pre-installed (Phase 1.2). Each of these
was addressed later; see the sections that follow, through "The
encryption plan completed".

## Encryption remediation, Phase 1.2: DuckDB extensions (2026-11-10)

**A concurrency defect found while preparing this phase, and fixed.**
The encrypted DuckDB connection pool (`DuckDBAdapter$pool()`) could
never open a second concurrent connection. Every connection in the
pool shares one in-process DuckDB instance, and each ran
`ATTACH ... (ENCRYPTION_KEY ...)` again; DuckDB rejected the second
attach with "Unique file handle conflict: ... already attached".
Verified by execution: the first checkout succeeded and the second
failed. Any multi-user application on an encrypted DuckDB pool would
have failed under the first overlapping request. The pool now
attaches once per instance and each connection only selects the
attached database; two concurrent connections now see each other's
writes, and the file still verifies as encrypted.

**Extensions.** The R duckdb package keeps extensions in a
per-session temporary directory, so every R session downloaded
`httpfs` (required for encrypted files) again, and `icu` (required by
`CURRENT_DATE`) on first use. That fails on hosts without internet
access, and downloading unpinned code into a validated system is a
change-control concern under §11.10(k). Configuration now accepts
`duckdb.extension_directory` (a persistent directory) and
`duckdb.allow_extension_download`, which defaults to `FALSE` under the
`regulated` profile. `install_duckdb_extensions()` populates the
directory on a connected machine and verifies an offline load in a
fresh instance. Extensions are loaded when a connection opens, so a
missing one is an error at startup, naming the remedy, rather than at
the first deadline query. Verified: with downloads disabled and a
pre-populated directory, an encrypted database opens and
`CURRENT_DATE` evaluates; with an empty directory, connection fails
with the documented message. 12 new assertions in
`inst/tinytest/test_duckdb_extensions.R`.

**A limitation this phase exposed (resolved the same day; see the
next section).** The shipped Shiny application could not use DuckDB
at all: `inst/app/global.R` built its connection pool directly with
RSQLite, and 25 application files received that pool.

## The application on the database adapter (2026-11-10)

The application now opens whichever backend `config.yml` selects.
`app_database_config()` translates the application's flat
`database:` section (`backend`, `path`, `encryption_key`,
`extension_directory`, server connection settings, `pool_size`) into
an adapter configuration; `global.R` builds its pool from that
adapter, applies the security profile to that backend before opening
it, and caches the adapter so that package functions the application
calls reach the same database. The launcher (`launch_zzedc()`) uses
the same configuration for its initialization check, first-time
initialization, and table migrations, which previously opened the
file with RSQLite whatever the configuration said.

**Defects found and fixed during the port.**

1. *Two in-process DuckDB instances on one file.* Every call to
   `DuckDBAdapter$connect()` created its own DuckDB instance. A
   package function called by the application (for example audit
   logging through `connect_encrypted_db()`) therefore attached the
   study file through a second instance while the application's pool
   held it through another; DuckDB's file lock is held per process
   and does not prevent this. Observed directly: with the pool open, a
   second instance attached and queried the same encrypted file. The
   adapter now keeps one shared instance for all its connections and
   its pool, with an explicit `shutdown()` for handing the file to
   another adapter. Verified: adapters for different files stay
   separate; a `connect()` connection and the pool see each other's
   writes; an externally shut-down instance is recreated.
2. *Audit tables never created at launch.* The launcher's default
   initialization created `audit_trail` but not `audit_log`, the
   hash-chained table that `log_audit_event()` and the login lockout
   events write to. On SQLite this was masked, because those package
   functions also opened a different file (`./data/zzedc.db` relative
   to the application directory) and failed there instead. The
   launcher now runs `init_audit_logging()` on the configured backend.
   Verified: a failed login is recorded in `audit_log` inside the
   encrypted DuckDB database, and `verify_audit_integrity()` passes.
3. *Keyless SQLite deployments could not use package functions.*
   `connect_encrypted_db()` demanded `DB_ENCRYPTION_KEY` even for a
   plaintext file, which needs no key; it now opens a plaintext file
   without one, still applying the security profile, and still
   requires a key for an encrypted file.
4. *The Admin tab backed up the wrong file.* `admin_dashboard_server()`
   was mounted without a database path, so its backup, restore, and
   database-information panels defaulted to `./data/zzedc.db` relative
   to the application directory, not the study database. The
   configured path is now passed. File backup is refused with an
   explanation on server backends, and DuckDB is checkpointed before
   copying.
5. *The `standard` profile's warning was invisible in a running
   application,* because R holds top-level warnings until the
   top-level call returns, and `launch_zzedc()` does not return while
   the application runs. It is now emitted immediately.
6. *One SQLite-only statement in the application path*
   (`date('now', '-30 days')` in the Compliance tab) was replaced with
   a cutoff computed in R.

**Live verification.** The installed package was launched with
`launch_zzedc()` in three configurations. Encrypted DuckDB under
`regulated`, with pre-installed extensions and downloads disabled:
the launcher created the encrypted study database and the application
served its page (HTTP 200). Plaintext SQLite under `regulated`: the
launcher refused before creating anything, stating the reason and the
remedy. SQLite under `standard`: the application started and logged
the warning. Separately, the application's own `global.R` and
`authenticate_user()` (from `inst/app/auth.R`) were run against an
encrypted DuckDB study database: a wrong password was rejected and
counted, the correct password succeeded with the forced password
change set, the failed attempt was written to the audit log, and the
file remained unreadable without the key. An interactive browser
session was not run (the browser automation extension was not
connected), so rendering and navigation of individual tabs on DuckDB
remain unverified.

**Left open at the time, fixed on 2026-11-11** (see "Follow-up fixes"
below): the Google Sheets actions were SQLite-only; the backup
module's restore copied over the open database and closed the shared
pool; and `initialize_default_database()` hashed the default
administrator's password with a different salt than the login used,
so that account could not log in whenever `ZZEDC_SALT` was set.

## Choosing the database when a study is created (2026-11-10)

Before this change, a new study's database could be chosen only by
editing `config.yml` by hand, and nothing explained the choice:
`launch_zzedc()` wrote a SQLite configuration (with no security
profile, so the `standard` default applied, contrary to the decision
that new configurations be `regulated`), and the setup wizard had no
database step.

**What exists now.** `describe_backends()` holds one description of
each backend (what it is, when to use it, how it encrypts stored
data, and whether the `regulated` profile accepts it), used by all
three entry points so they cannot drift apart. `launch_zzedc()` in a
directory without `config.yml` prints that comparison and asks which
backend to use, or offers the browser wizard; `launch_zzedc(backend =
...)` skips the question. Choosing DuckDB checks for the encryption
key first (in an interactive session it generates one, shows it once,
and offers to add it to `~/.Renviron`, outside the project; it is
never written to the project directory), then installs DuckDB's
extensions for offline use, and only then writes `config.yml`, so a
failure leaves no half-created study. Choosing SQLite under
`regulated` without an encrypting RSQLite asks whether the study needs
encrypted storage, and either points to DuckDB or records the
`standard` profile.

**The setup wizard is now reachable and works.** It is opened with
`launch_setup_wizard()` or `launch_zzedc(setup = TRUE)`. It gained a
security-profile choice and a Database step with a hover summary for
each option, a comparison table, a check of the choice against the
profile (it will not continue with a combination that would refuse to
start), a generated DuckDB key that must be confirmed as saved, and
server connection settings. Its **Launch ZZedc** button starts the new
study in the same session.

**Defects found and fixed in the wizard.**

1. *Create Study created nothing.* The final step's handler contained
   a placeholder comment and showed the success panel without calling
   `complete_wizard_setup()`. It now creates the study and reports
   each step's failure if one occurs.
2. *The wizard's `config.yml` could not be read.* `create_wizard_config()`
   wrote its settings at the top level; `config::get()`, which the
   launcher and the application use, rejects such a file ("You must
   provide a default configuration"). It now writes under `default:`,
   and quotes free-text values, so a study name containing a colon no
   longer breaks the file.
3. *The launch script opened the wrong directory.* It called
   `launch_zzedc()` from wherever it was run, which creates a new
   default study there. It now changes to the study directory first,
   and for DuckDB checks for the key.
4. *The data-source options were never carried out.* The last step
   offered example forms, CSV import, and Google Sheets import, none
   of which the setup function implemented. It now states that the
   study is created without forms and how to add them.
5. The security salt was generated with `sample()`, which is not a
   cryptographic random source; it now comes from `openssl`.

**Verification.** 61 assertions in
`inst/tinytest/test_backend_setup.R`, including a `shiny::testServer()`
walk through all six steps that creates an encrypted DuckDB study and
checks that the wizard refuses a server database under `regulated` and
an unconfirmed key. With the installed package: the wizard page
rendered (HTTP 200) with all six steps and nine tooltips;
`launch_zzedc(backend = "duckdb")` with a key set installed the
extensions, wrote a `regulated` DuckDB configuration, created the
encrypted database, and served the application; without a key it
stopped with instructions and wrote nothing. Not verified: the
interactive console menu (it needs a terminal) and clicking through
the wizard in a browser (the browser automation extension was not
connected). The full test suite (3,910 assertions) shows no change
from the unchanged code except the new tests, and
`R CMD check --as-cran` reports 0 errors, 0 warnings, and 1 note (new
submission; one redirected URL).

**Left open at the time:** a separate first-run choice screen
(`setup_choice_module.R`) was not mounted anywhere; it is now the
first page of `launch_setup_wizard()` (see the next section).

## Follow-up fixes (2026-11-11)

**One password-salt rule.** Passwords were hashed with at least four
different salt rules: the login and the change-password form used the
configuration's salt variable, falling back to its default salt; the
launcher's default administrator used the package's built-in salt; the
Admin tab's user creation and password reset used `ZZEDC_SALT` or the
literal `"default_salt"`; the Google Sheets builders used
`"zzedc_default_salt"`. Accounts made by one path could fail to log in
through another: the default administrator whenever `ZZEDC_SALT` was
set, and users created in the Admin tab whenever the configuration
named no salt variable. `resolve_auth_salt()` is now the single rule;
the application sets it once at startup, and the launcher, login,
change-password form, and user management all use it. Verified: with a
custom `ZZEDC_SALT`, a study created by `launch_zzedc()` accepts the
default administrator through the application's own login function.

**Restore is staged and applied at startup.** The database cannot be
replaced while the application holds it open. Restore now checks the
backup (it must be a database of the study's backend) and stages it;
`apply_pending_restore()`, called by the launcher and the application
before any connection opens, keeps the current database and its
write-ahead log, removes the old log, and swaps the file. Verified on
SQLite (including a compressed backup and a stale write-ahead log) and
on encrypted DuckDB, which remained encrypted. Three further defects in
the backup module were fixed: SQLite backups are made with
`VACUUM INTO` rather than a file copy that could miss commits still in
the write-ahead log; "compressed" backups were never compressed (a
file named `.gz` held an uncompressed copy, which a restore then failed
to decompress); and backups were written into the installed package's
directory, where a reinstall deleted them. A security defect was also
fixed: the backup paths sent by the browser were used as given, so a
crafted message could restore from, or delete, any file the
application could reach; only files in the backup folder are now
accepted.

**Google Sheets import on every backend.** The application's Google
Sheets actions sourced a setup script from the application directory,
which does not contain it, so they failed on every backend; the legacy
builders behind them rebuilt SQLite tables. The actions now call
`setup_zzedc_from_gsheets()`, which gained `adapter_config` (any
backend) and `create_database = FALSE` (import into an existing study,
skipping users and forms that already exist rather than failing or
overwriting). Inside the application it reuses the application's own
database adapter, so on DuckDB the import shares the connection pool's
database instance rather than attaching the study file a second time.
Fixing this exposed a data-model defect: imported fields
are attached to a form by `crf_definitions.crf_id`, but the schema
declares `designer_fields.design_id` a foreign key to `designer_forms`.
SQLite does not enforce that by default, so every import on SQLite
wrote fields that point at a design that does not exist, and on
backends that enforce foreign keys (DuckDB, PostgreSQL) every imported
field was rejected. The importers (Google Sheets and REDCap) now create
the matching `designer_forms` row, and `create_designer_form()` assigns
ids above any existing one so the two cannot collide. Verified with the
Google Sheets reader replaced by fixed tables: on encrypted DuckDB an
import adds new users and a form with its fields and choice options,
a second import adds nothing and reports no errors, and an existing
user's password is not reset. A live import against Google Sheets was
not run.

**First-run choice screen.** It is now the first page of
`launch_setup_wizard()`, offering the wizard or the console commands,
with its content corrected (six steps, current commands, and no
placeholder links or example email address).

**Later the same day.** The legacy Google Sheets pipeline was removed:
the three builder files in `inst/app/`, the setup scripts that called
them (`inst/scripts/setup/setup_from_gsheets.R` and `setup_menu.R`),
and a disabled test of them. They hashed passwords with a fixed salt
shared by every installation (accounts they created could not log in)
and rebuilt tables in place. The application's "Run Traditional Setup"
button, which sourced a script the application directory does not
contain, was removed. The technical-lead guide had documented a CSV
setup path, `setup_zzedc_from_csv()`, that did not exist; it now
exists, sharing the Google Sheets importer's logic, so the same three
tables can be loaded from local files on any backend. Importing into
an existing study now also skips validation rules already present, and
honors the documented `active` column (it was ignored) and a new
optional `form_name` column.

**The bundled example study.** `inst/extdata/adhd_trial`, a fictional
ADHD medication trial, was in a format only the removed scripts could
read. It was converted to the three-table format (nine forms, 129
fields, 57 validation rules, four demonstration accounts) and loads
completely with `setup_zzedc_from_csv()` on SQLite and on encrypted
DuckDB. One display condition, on a field whose controlling field is on
another form, could not be expressed as a rule and was dropped; a form
listed in the old example but never defined was also dropped.

**Remaining.** The Backup tab's Download button had no handler; it was
fixed in the next section.

## The encryption plan completed (2026-11-11)

This section records the remaining phases of the encryption and
compliance plan except Phase 5 (Part 11 gaps), which is being
addressed separately.

**Backups and the Backup tab.** Backups of a database that is not
encrypted at rest held every record in readable form. With
`ZZEDC_BACKUP_PASSPHRASE` set, backups are now encrypted with the same
authenticated scheme as exports, under a passphrase held apart from
the database key; under `regulated`, an unencrypted backup of an
unencrypted database is refused before anything is written. The
Download button, which did nothing, now serves the selected backup
and records an `EXPORT` audit event.

**HTTPS.** The `https_only` setting existed in `config.yml` but nothing
read it. The application now blocks sessions that did not arrive over
HTTPS when `https_only` is set and always under `regulated`. Because
Shiny does not terminate TLS, HTTPS comes from a reverse proxy; the
proxy's `X-Forwarded-Proto` header is believed only when the request
came from the same machine, since a client reaching the application
directly could otherwise claim HTTPS by sending the header.

**Keys.** A key written into `config.yml` defeats encryption for
anyone who can read the project; it is now refused under `regulated`.
Each start records in the audit log that the key was loaded and from
where. `rotate_database_key()` re-encrypts a DuckDB database by copying
it into a new file under the new key, verifying the copy, and only
then swapping it in, keeping the old file until the operator removes
it. The documentation states what the software cannot do: recover a
lost key.

**Server databases.** Until now `regulated` refused PostgreSQL and
MySQL/MariaDB outright, because their storage encryption is not
visible to zzedc. MySQL and MariaDB report, per InnoDB tablespace,
whether it is encrypted, and zzedc now checks every table of the study
database. Community PostgreSQL reports nothing comparable, so the
deployer records the mechanism as `at_rest_attestation`; zzedc accepts
it under `regulated` and labels it everywhere as attested. Both
require a TLS mode that verifies the server and a live connection that
uses TLS. No database server was available for this work, so the
decision logic is tested against a fake adapter; the SQL queries sent
to real servers have not been executed.

**Evidence.** Each start of the application writes a
`COMPLIANCE_CHECK` audit event stating the security configuration in
force, including the basis of the at-rest claim (package-enforced,
server-verified, server-attested, or none). The record is protected by
the audit hash chain rather than by a separate signature. Operational
qualification gains OQ-011 to OQ-018, one per security control. Four
documents for reviewers are installed under
`system.file("compliance", package = "zzedc")`: a responsibility
matrix covering Part 11, HIPAA 164.312, and GDPR Article 32(1); a HIPAA
encryption worksheet; a GDPR Article 32 statement template; and a
one-page IRB security summary.

**Not verified here.** The SQLite cipher route (Phase 1.1) is
documented with build steps but was not exercised, as no cipher-enabled
RSQLite was available. The OQ tests target the behavior each control
replaced but were not run against the pre-fix code.

## The audit trail against 21 CFR 11.10(e) (2026-11-11)

A review of the audit trail against 11.10(e) and HIPAA 164.312(b)
found that its design (a SHA-256 chain whose hashes recompute from the
stored rows) was sound but that it did not cover, or protect, what
those provisions require.

**Coverage.** The EDC tab saved case report form entries with no audit
record at all; the audit trail recorded signatures, corrections, and
security events, but not the primary data. Each entry is now written
together with an `INSERT` audit record (submitted values, user, UTC
time, client address, session) in one transaction, so neither can
commit without the other. Successful logins, attempts on unknown or
locked accounts, logoffs, and session ends are now recorded; before,
only wrong passwords and lockouts were. Automatic logoff, which
existed as code but was never activated and could not have fired, now
works and is recorded.

**Failure.** Every audit writer caught its own errors and issued a
warning, and callers discarded even that, so an action whose audit
record failed proceeded unrecorded. Under `regulated`, a failed audit
write is now an error, and a login that cannot be recorded is refused.

**Protection.** Nothing prevented the application's own database
account from changing or deleting audit rows, and an internal
maintenance function deleted rows older than a year. The hash chain
detects an edit only if the editor does not recompute the later
hashes; with write access, recomputing them is straightforward, and a
test in the suite now demonstrates it. Three layers apply instead:
the chain; triggers that make the audit tables append-only on SQLite,
PostgreSQL, and MySQL/MariaDB; and keyed checkpoints of the chain's
head written outside the database, which detect a rewrite up to the
latest checkpoint even when every hash was recomputed. DuckDB supports
no triggers, so there the checkpoints carry the protection. A database
administrator can still drop triggers; the remaining defense is
privilege separation on server backends and frequent checkpoints to
storage the database host cannot rewrite, both deployer
responsibilities.

**Review.** The Admin tab's audit viewer read a table that nothing in
the application wrote, and when its query failed it displayed twenty
randomly generated entries as though they were the study's audit
trail. It now reads the chained log, and shows an error when it cannot.
Its table rendered audit content as raw HTML; since failed logins now
record the username as typed, that would have let a crafted username
run script in an administrator's browser, so all content is escaped.

**Corrections.** The correction workflow recorded each correction's
old value, new value, reason, and approval, marked it applied, and
wrote an audit record saying the value had changed, but never changed
the stored value; its lock check also read a field the lock function
does not return, so locked records were never protected. A correction
now changes the field and writes its audit record in one transaction,
refuses a request whose original value no longer matches the record,
and requires an approved override for a locked record.

**Not done.** Reads of records are not logged. The triggers and the
chain lock on PostgreSQL and MySQL are untested against live servers.
The REDCap importer's replay of historical audit events still writes
the chain through its own code, without the lock.

## Comparison with REDCap and other EDC platforms, condensed

REDCap is the natural reference point. The two systems address a
similar problem space and have substantially overlapping feature sets
in routine data capture. Differences worth naming:

REDCap is licensed by the Vanderbilt consortium and redistribution is
restricted to consortium members; ZZedc is released under an
open-source license. REDCap's compliance posture is presented at the
institutional level (the institution running REDCap is the
controller); ZZedc's compliance posture is tied to specific exported
functions in inspectable R code. REDCap extends through PHP modules;
ZZedc extends through R packages. REDCap has been deployed at
institutional scale for over a decade and has correspondingly mature
operations tooling; ZZedc is a newer system and its operational
maturity is less battle-tested. REDCap's implementation of GDPR data
subject rights is module-level; ZZedc implements each right as a
dedicated function set with cited line numbers and tinytests.

No EDC platform in this comparison, REDCap included, makes installing
or running the software alone sufficient for 21 CFR Part 11, HIPAA, or
GDPR compliance. Compliance in every case examined resolves to the
same three layers: validated or validatable technical controls in the
software, environment and procedure supplied by the deploying
institution, and configuration and execution records supplied by the
individual study. Institutions hosting the identical REDCap codebase
have published materially different public answers to 'is this Part
11 compliant', ranging from an unqualified 'fully complies' to 'has
not been validated; consider a different product', which is itself
evidence that the determination is institutional, not a property of
any one platform's code. OpenClinica markets its hosted, paid tier as
'compliant from day one' but makes no equivalent claim for its free,
self-hosted Community Edition. Castor EDC publishes a versioned '21
CFR Part 11 Statement of Compliance' tied to each named software
release, naming the customer explicitly as the party the statement
binds; this is the most disciplined documentation practice found
across the platforms surveyed and a model ZZedc's own compliance
documentation should move toward, rather than relying on a single
internal markdown file. LibreClinica, a community fork of
OpenClinica's original architecture, carries no compliance
documentation of any kind in the sources reviewed.

A separate question, often skipped by institutions and vendors alike,
is whether 21 CFR Part 11 even applies to a given study. Part 11
binds records required under an FDA predicate rule; most
investigator-initiated academic trials are not conducted under an IND
or IDE, in which case the governing requirements are more likely to
be the HIPAA Security Rule, institutional data-security policy, and
GDPR Article 32, not Part 11's electronic-signature and audit-trail
provisions. A funder's or sponsor's contractual terms can still impose
Part-11-like obligations independent of FDA law, so this is a
determination to make deliberately for each study rather than an
assumption to carry over from a prior IND-governed trial.

The choice among these platforms is largely an institutional one.
ZZedc is a defensible choice when source-level inspection of
compliance code matters, when integration with R-based downstream
analysis is the dominant workflow, when consortium licensing is
unavailable, or when the deploying organization needs to extend or
modify compliance behavior rather than configure it within fixed
parameters. REDCap is the conservative default at institutions that
already license it and have an established operational practice
around it; switching to ZZedc has a justified case but is not a
default recommendation. Prospective adopters should also weigh that
ZZedc does not yet have a Castor-style versioned compliance statement
of its own; the gap-analysis addendum and encryption-remediation
sections below are the closest current substitute, and are a less
mature artifact than what institutions have come to expect from
REDCap's consortium validation process or Castor's per-release
statement.
